title: You're Self-Aware. So Why Do You Keep Repeating the Same Patterns?
seoTitle: Why Self-Awareness Isn't Enough to Change Your Behaviour
excerpt: Understand why recognising your unhealthy patterns doesn't automatically change them, when intellectualising becomes avoidance, and how CBT behavioural experiments turn insight into action.
homeExcerpt: You can name your attachment style and perfectionism and still repeat them. Why insight isn't the mechanism, and how CBT bridges the gap.
llmsTitle: Why Self-Awareness Isn't Enough to Change Your Behaviour
llmsSummary: Explains the self-awareness paradox: why naming attachment styles, perfectionism or cognitive distortions explains a pattern without interrupting it, and how intellectualising emotions ('Why am I like this?') can become unconstructive repetitive thought and avoidance (Watkins, 2008). Compares mindset change to physical training and shows how CBT behavioural experiments (Beck, 2020; Healthdirect Australia; NHS) test predictions in small real-world situations (e.g. politely declining one request to test 'people will stop liking me'), plus a five-question behavioural progress checklist.

title: Why Do You Keep Repeating the Same Patterns Even When You Know Better?
seoTitle: Why Do I Keep Repeating the Same Patterns? A CBT Guide to Self-Sabotage
excerpt: Understand the psychology behind self-sabotage, avoidance and recurring behaviour — the short-term emotional protection behind six common habits, and five CBT steps for building a different response.
homeExcerpt: Self-sabotage often persists because it delivers immediate protection from discomfort. The hidden rewards behind six habits, and five CBT steps to break them.
llmsTitle: Why Do I Keep Repeating the Same Patterns? A CBT Guide to Self-Sabotage
llmsSummary: Examines recurring behavioural patterns as short-term emotional self-protection rather than a discipline failure. Maps six behaviours in a structured table (people-pleasing, perfectionism, overthinking, emotional withdrawal, reassurance-seeking, procrastination) by short-term reward and long-term cost, traces the CBT trigger-thought-emotion-avoidance-relief cycle (Beck, 2020; Healthdirect Australia; NHS), outlines a five-step method for testing manageable alternatives, and explains why healthy unfamiliar responses initially feel uncomfortable.

title: Manifestation vs CBT: Why Imagining a Better Life Isn't the Same as Building One
seoTitle: Manifestation vs CBT: The Difference Between Believing and Changing
excerpt: Discover the psychological differences between manifestation and cognitive behavioural therapy, why idealised positive fantasies can sap motivation, and how to pair future goals with CBT action.
homeExcerpt: Imagining a better future feels rewarding, which is sometimes why it stalls action. How manifestation and CBT differ, and how to confront what's stopping you.
llmsTitle: Manifestation vs CBT: The Difference Between Believing and Changing
llmsSummary: Compares manifestation and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) across five mechanisms. Reviews Gabriele Oettingen's research showing that idealised positive fantasies without obstacle awareness can sap physiological energy and effort toward goals (Oettingen & Mayer, 2002; Kappes & Oettingen, 2011), contrasts affirmation repetition with CBT belief-testing questions, and demonstrates how combining a meaningful future direction with small behavioural experiments (such as applying for one role to test fear of rejection) builds genuine confidence.

title: Journaling vs CBT: Why Writing About Your Problems Isn't Always Enough
seoTitle: Journaling vs CBT: Why Writing About Your Problems Isn't Always Enough
excerpt: Learn the difference between traditional journaling and CBT thought records, when free-form venting turns into rumination, and how structured reflection challenges recurring patterns.
llmsTitle: Journaling vs CBT: Why Writing About Your Problems Isn't Always Enough
llmsSummary: Contrasts open-ended emotional journaling with structured CBT thought records. Explains when repetitive 'why me?' writing becomes unconstructive rumination (Watkins, 2008), walks through an eight-part CBT thought record table for an unanswered message (situation, automatic thought, emotion, distortion, evidence for/against, balanced interpretation, behavioural response; Beck, 2020; NHS), and shows how journaling and CBT complement each other.

title: CBT vs Positive Thinking: You Don't Need to Convince Yourself Everything Is Okay
seoTitle: CBT vs Positive Thinking: Why You Don't Always Need a Positive Mindset
excerpt: Discover why cognitive behavioural therapy focuses on realistic, balanced thinking rather than forced positivity, how emotional reasoning works, and six questions for cognitive restructuring.
llmsTitle: CBT vs Positive Thinking: Why You Don't Always Need a Positive Mindset
llmsSummary: Clarifies why CBT teaches realistic, balanced interpretations rather than forced optimism. Contrasts automatic self-condemnation and unbelievable positive slogans with a balanced workplace-mistake reframe, explains emotional reasoning (treating feelings as proof of external facts), provides a six-question cognitive restructuring checklist (Beck, 2020; NHS; Healthdirect Australia), and frames mental resilience as cognitive flexibility rather than constant happiness.

title: CBT Tools Compared: How to Choose a CBT App (and Why Reframed Is Built for Mindset)
excerpt: Paper workbooks, MindShift CBT, Clarity, Wysa, and Reframed compared by mechanism, privacy, and cost — plus why shifting a mindset is a different job from mood tracking or open-ended chat.
llmsTitle: CBT Tools Compared: How to Choose a CBT App (and Why Reframed Is Built for Mindset)
llmsSummary: Criteria-based comparison of CBT tools in 2026 (published by Hexp Studios, maker of Reframed). Reviews meta-analytic evidence for CBT smartphone apps across 176 RCTs (Linardon et al., World Psychiatry, 2024: g = 0.28 depression, g = 0.26 anxiety; active CBT outperforms passive mood tracking). Compares five categories in a structured table: Reframed (iOS, on-device storage, personality-matched 2-min prompts, distortion detection, 5-step thought records, belief evidence log, no streaks, Pro subscription or lifetime purchase), MindShift CBT (Anxiety Canada, iOS/Android, 100% free, strong for worry and phobia fear ladders), Clarity (iOS/Android freemium journaling and CBT courses), Wysa (iOS/Android freemium AI chatbot and coaching; notes Woebot retired its standalone consumer app on 30 June 2025), and paper workbooks (CCI, Mind Over Mood). Explains why mindset/self-image change requires falsifiable evidence logging rather than affirmations (Wood et al., 2009) or reassurance chat, and specifies when other tools or licensed therapy are a better fit.

title: How CBT Apps Build Emotional Resilience and Emotional Intelligence
excerpt: Resilience isn't feeling nothing, and emotional intelligence isn't a fixed gift. How emotion granularity and early cognitive reappraisal work, and how daily CBT practice trains both.
llmsTitle: How CBT Apps Build Emotional Resilience and Emotional Intelligence
llmsSummary: How structured CBT app practice develops emotional intelligence (Mayer & Salovey, 1997 four-branch ability model) and psychological resilience. Reviews three meta-analyses confirming EI is trainable in adults (Hodzic et al., 2018; Mattingly & Kraiger, 2019; Kotsou et al., 2019), Gross & John (2003) on cognitive reappraisal outperforming expressive suppression, Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight (2015) on emotion differentiation (emotional granularity), and Troy, Shallcross & Mauss (2013) on why reappraisal helps with uncontrollable stressors while controllable problems require pairing accurate reframes with action. Maps four app mechanics (precise emotion naming, catching interpersonal distortions like mind reading, early setback reappraisal, and longitudinal pattern tracking) to real-world resilience and relationship skills.
homeExcerpt: Resilience isn't feeling nothing, and emotional intelligence isn't fixed. How naming precise feelings and catching distortions early train both.

title: How to Use a CBT App to Stop Self-Sabotaging (Without Turning the App Into Another Trap)
excerpt: Why streak-based habit trackers backfire on perfectionists, and a four-step way to catch permission-giving excuses on your phone right before you bail.
llmsTitle: How to Use a CBT App to Stop Self-Sabotaging (Without Turning the App Into Another Trap)
llmsSummary: Operational guide to interrupting self-sabotage in real time on a smartphone. Explains why phones sit at the short-term mood-repair point of procrastination (Sirois & Pychyl, 2013), why streak counters and complex task trackers backfire via all-or-nothing thinking, and gives a four-step live protocol: log Judith Beck's 'permission-giving thoughts' verbatim, name the avoided emotion and distortion, write a reframe acknowledging the self-handicapping payoff (Berglas & Jones, 1978), and exit into a two-minute behavioural experiment (Bennett-Levy et al., 2004; Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006). Includes playbooks for last-minute stalling, endless polishing (99%), research spirals, and pulling away in relationships, plus four rules so reflection doesn't become productive procrastination.

title: Ten Everyday Thinking Traps, and a Reframe for Each
excerpt: The unanswered message, the meeting with no agenda, the skipped workout. Ten familiar moments, the thought each one produces, and a version you can believe.
llmsTitle: Ten Everyday Thinking Traps, and a Reframe for Each
llmsSummary: A short guide in three levels. Basics: what a cognitive distortion is, why thinking patterns become automatic, and what a believable reframe looks like. Everyday: mind reading, catastrophising, all-or-nothing thinking and emotional reasoning. Deeper: rigid 'should' rules, core beliefs, and testing a prediction with a small behavioural experiment. Each entry has a situation, the automatic thought, a balanced reframe and one practice step. Further reading from NHS Every Mind Matters, HealthyWA and the Centre for Clinical Interventions.

title: How to Stop Self-Sabotaging: What CBT Says About the Pattern
excerpt: Procrastination, half-finished work, pulling away when things go well. Why self-sabotage protects you from a feeling, and a five-step way to catch your own pattern before it runs.
llmsTitle: How to Stop Self-Sabotaging: What CBT Says About the Pattern
llmsSummary: Self-sabotage as a protective pattern rather than a willpower problem. Covers self-handicapping (Berglas & Jones, 1978), procrastination as short-term mood repair (Sirois & Pychyl, 2013), the CBT layers of core belief, rule and automatic thought, five common forms with the thought behind each, a five-step practice (name the behaviour, rewind to the trigger, write the thought, find the payoff, test and plan), and if-then implementation intentions (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006).
homeExcerpt: Self-sabotage isn't a willpower problem. Why it protects you from a feeling, and how to catch your own pattern before it runs.

title: 12 Cognitive Biases Shaping How We Think in 2026
excerpt: Confirmation bias, automation bias, the illusory truth effect and nine more: what each one is, a 2026 example, and what it costs us.
llmsTitle: 12 Cognitive Biases Shaping How We Think in 2026
llmsSummary: Confirmation bias, negativity bias, social comparison, availability bias, in-group bias, authority and automation bias, fundamental attribution error, survivorship bias, anchoring, sunk cost fallacy, overconfidence/Dunning–Kruger, and the illusory truth effect, each with a definition, a 2026 example and its impact. Context from the Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026 (54% use social/video networks for news, 62% concerned about fake news, 10% use AI chatbots for news weekly; 48 markets), with the caveat that these figures don't show biases have increased (Budak et al., Nature, 2024).

title: Cognitive Biases vs Cognitive Distortions: What's the Difference?
excerpt: Two lists of thinking errors from two research traditions. How they differ, where they overlap, and which ten to work on first.
llmsSummary: Biases come from judgment and decision-making research (Kahneman and Tversky); distortions come from CBT (Beck). How they overlap, and ten thinking patterns ranked for everyday use: start with negativity bias, confirmation bias, catastrophising, mind reading, all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralisation and social comparison.

title: Five Thinking Patterns to Catch First
excerpt: Catastrophising, mind reading, all-or-nothing thinking, confirmation bias and overgeneralisation, each with the one question that tests it.
llmsTitle: Five Thinking Patterns to Catch First
llmsSummary: Catastrophising, mind reading, all-or-nothing thinking, confirmation bias and overgeneralisation, each with a plain test question and a worked reframe. Recommends learning the pattern before the psychological term.

title: Psycho-Cybernetics and CBT: How to Actually Change Your Self-Image
excerpt: Maxwell Maltz said your self-image sets the limits of what you'll do. How his idea maps onto CBT, what the research says about changing a mindset, and the daily practice that does the changing.
llmsTitle: Psycho-Cybernetics and CBT: How to Actually Change Your Self-Image
llmsSummary: How Maxwell Maltz's idea of the self-image (Psycho-Cybernetics, 1960) maps onto CBT core beliefs and automatic thoughts; what the evidence says about changing a mindset (Hofmann et al. 2012 on CBT, Lally et al. 2009 on the 66-day habit average versus the "21 days" myth, Sisk et al. 2018 on growth-mindset interventions); and the catch-name-test-rewrite practice. Bridges readers of Maltz, Dweck, Clear and the Stoics to CBT.
homeExcerpt: Maltz said your self-image sets the limits. How that maps onto CBT, what the evidence says about changing a mindset, and the practice that does it.

title: The 10 Cognitive Distortions, With Examples
excerpt: All-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising, mind reading — the ten patterns CBT names, what each one sounds like in your own head, and the question that breaks it.
llmsSummary: The ten distortions catalogued in CBT — all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralisation, mental filter, discounting the positive, jumping to conclusions, magnification/minimisation, emotional reasoning, "should" statements, labelling, personalisation — each with an example thought and a challenge question.
homeExcerpt: All-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising, mind reading — the ten patterns CBT names, what each sounds like in your own head, and the question that breaks it.

title: How to Write a CBT Thought Record
excerpt: The core exercise of cognitive behavioural therapy, in five columns. A worked example from a bad Tuesday, plus the four mistakes that make a thought record useless.
llmsTitle: How to Write a CBT Thought Record
llmsSummary: The five-column thought record (situation, automatic thought, emotion, distortion, balanced thought), a worked example, and four common mistakes.
homeExcerpt: The core exercise of cognitive behavioural therapy, in five columns. A worked example, plus the four mistakes that make a thought record useless.

title: Why Affirmations Don't Work — And What Does
excerpt: Repeating "I am capable" to a brain that believes otherwise starts an argument you lose. What the research says, and the order of operations that actually shifts a belief.
llmsTitle: Why Affirmations Don't Work — And What Does
llmsSummary: Why positive self-statements backfire for people with low self-esteem (Wood, Perunovic & Lee, 2009), and why cognitive reframing addresses the existing belief instead of layering a new one on top.
homeExcerpt: Repeating "I am capable" to a brain that believes otherwise starts an argument you lose. What the research says, and what shifts a belief instead.
